title: [Feature]: show guest OS in cubic instances
body:
## Feature Description

Show the guest OS in the `cubic instances` list.

## Use Case

Right now there is no way to tell which OS an instance runs without connecting to it. Showing the OS at a glance helps when managing many instances.

## Proposed Solution

Add an `os` field to `instance.toml`.

At instance creation, leave it empty since the OS is not known yet.

When a user connects to a VM with ssh, scp, or exec, read `/etc/os-release` over SFTP using the same credentials and update `os` in `instance.toml` from the `ID` and `VERSION_ID` fields, formatted as `ID:VERSION_ID`, for example `ubuntu:22.04`. We may want a minimum time between refreshes to avoid reading the file on every connect, exact interval to be decided.

If the read fails or the file is missing, leave the existing stored value untouched.

In `cubic instances`, show the stored `os` value, or an empty column for instances that have none, including ones created before this change.

## Feature Description

Cubic should automatically generate a VM instance name when the user does not provide one. The name should follow an `adjective + noun` format, similar to Docker's automatically generated names. If the user provides a name, Cubic should use it instead.

## Use Case

The `create` and `run` command should make the VM instance name optional:

title: refactor: share the terminal and let each view own its line
body:
## Summary

Reworks how the live terminal line is driven. The console keeps one frame and each view pushes its own frame to it, replacing the single render thread that polled whichever `Animation` trait object had been registered along with the `play` and `stop` pair callers used to hand an animation over. A spinner owns its tick thread and lives as a scoped guard, and the transfer views render straight into the console as bytes arrive.

The point of the change is that whatever shows a line owns it. A spinner clears its line when it goes out of scope, so a command ends on a clean line whether it returns normally, returns early or fails, where before each caller had to pair a stop call with the spinner it started. Messages printed while a spinner runs land above the live line, and a password prompt during `cubic ssh` takes the line and gives it back once it is answered.

Frames now also go out through `System` like every other write, which brings the console's terminal output under test for the first time. Sharing the console as an `Arc` in the first commit is the prerequisite for a view holding on to the console it draws through.

title: [Feature]: Show live memory usage of a running VM
body:
## Feature Description

Show how much memory a running VM is actually using, next to the memory it
was given. In `cubic show <vm>` and in the `cubic instances` list, display
the memory a VM really uses, the same way disk already shows `4/100 G`.

## Use Case

Today Cubic only shows the memory a VM was configured with. There is no way
to tell how much of it the VM is really using without opening a shell inside
the guest and running a tool like `free`.

Seeing used memory at a glance helps you:

- Spot a VM that is running low on memory
- Notice a VM that was given far more than it needs
- Right size your VMs when running several at once

## Proposed Solution

- In `cubic instances`, the Memory column reads `512/2048 M`, matching the disk column style.
- In `cubic show <vm>`, a `Memory used` line shows the used memory, for example `Memory used: 512 M`.
- Used counts memory the workload really holds and leaves out reclaimable cache, so a healthy VM does not look full.
- Stopped VMs and VMs that cannot report usage keep showing the configured memory as before.

title: [Feature]: Add Setup Dialog
body:
## Feature Description

An interactive setup screen for the VM settings. It shows every setting in one form so the user can move up and down and change values in any order. Launch it with `cubic create --setup` or `cubic modify --setup`.

## Use Case

Today every setting is a command line flag. A new user has to read the help output first and then guess good values for CPUs, memory and disk. Changing a setting later means writing another modify command with the right flag names. A form shows the current values, tells the user what the host can give and lets the user go back and forth until the settings look right.

## Proposed Solution

### Create, advanced collapsed

```
╭─ Create VM instance ─────────────────────────────╮
│                                                  │
│    Image     ‹ ubuntu:latest ›                   │
│  ▸ vCPUs     ‹ 4 ›            4 of 8             │
│    Memory    ‹ 4G ›           4G of 16G          │
│    Disk      ‹ 100G ›         42G free           │
│                                                  │
│    ▸ Advanced                                    │
│                                                  │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│    ⟨ Create ⟩    ⟨ Cancel ⟩                      │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
  ↑↓ field   ←→ change   ⏎ edit   esc cancel
```

### Create, advanced expanded

```
╭─ Create VM instance ─────────────────────────────╮
│                                                  │
│    Image     ‹ ubuntu:latest ›                   │
│    vCPUs     ‹ 4 ›            4 of 8             │
│    Memory    ‹ 4G ›           4G of 16G          │
│    Disk      ‹ 100G ›         42G free           │
│                                                  │
│    ▾ Advanced                                    │
│                                                  │
│      User    ‹ cubic ›                           │
│    ▸ Ports     8000:80, 5353:53/udp          (2) │
│      Isolate ☐  no network access                │
│      Run       none                              │
│                                                  │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│    ⟨ Create ⟩    ⟨ Cancel ⟩                      │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
  ↑↓ field   ⏎ open list   esc cancel
```

The advanced section keeps the four core settings in front and holds everything else one keystroke away. It stays open for the rest of the session once the user expands it.

### Modify

```
╭─ Modify VM instance web ─────────────────────────╮
│                                                  │
│    Image       ubuntu:noble                      │
│  ▸ vCPUs     ‹ 4 ›            4 of 8             │
│    Memory    ‹ 4G ›           4G of 16G          │
│    Disk      ‹ 100G ›         42G free, min 100G │
│                                                  │
│    ▾ Advanced                                    │
│                                                  │
│      User      cubic                             │
│      Ports     8000:80                       (1) │
│      Isolate ☑  no network access                │
│      Run       none                              │
│                                                  │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│    ⟨ Save ⟩      ⟨ Cancel ⟩                      │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
  ↑↓ field   ←→ change   ⏎ edit   esc cancel
```

Image and user are fixed once an instance exists. They stay on screen as dimmed rows so the user still sees what the instance runs and the cursor skips over them. The disk row has a minimum of the current size so it can grow but never shrink.

### List editor

Ports and first boot commands are lists. The row shows a summary and a count. Enter opens the same list panel for both.

```
╭─ Port forwarding ────────────────────────────────╮
│                                                  │
│  ▸ 8000:80                                       │
│    5353:53/udp                                   │
│                                                  │
│    + add rule                                    │
│                                                  │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
  ↑↓ rule   ⏎ edit   a add   d delete   esc back
```

### Image picker

```
╭─ Select image ───────────────── ‹ deb        › ──╮
│                                                  │
│  ▸ debian:stable                                 │
│    debian:latest                                 │
│    debian:trixie                                 │
│    debian:bookworm                               │
│                                                  │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
  ↑↓ image   ⏎ select   type to filter   esc back
```

Left and right on the image row step through a few common images. Enter opens the full list and typing filters it.

### Text field

Enter on a scalar row opens a field for any value the steppers do not offer.

```

title: fix: end an ssh session without waiting for a key press
body:
## Summary

Closing an SSH session left cubic running until the user pressed a key. Dropping a tokio runtime waits for its blocking tasks to finish, and the stdin read behind `tokio::io::stdin()` can never be cancelled, so the process sat in that wait after the remote end had already closed. The async caller now shuts its runtime down on drop instead of waiting for it.

This restores the behaviour the async caller had before b29b171, which removed the explicit `shutdown_background()` call when `call` started serving two invocations per command. The same hang affected `cubic console`, which uses the same stdin relay, and it is fixed by the same change.

Tokio documents this trap on `tokio::io::stdin` and it has been open upstream for years in tokio-rs/tokio#589 and tokio-rs/tokio#2466.

title: perf: speed up the first boot of a VM instance
body:
## Summary

Cloud init generated an RSA, an ECDSA and an ed25519 host key on the first boot of every VM instance, and sshd could not start until all three existed. The seed now asks for an ed25519 key alone, which is the only key cubic ever uses, because it pins whatever key the guest offers on the first connect. The root filesystem also grows in the background now instead of blocking the cloud init network stage, since cubic always resizes the disk on create and that work always has something to do.

Together this takes about two and a half seconds off the time until a new VM instance answers on SSH.

This only affects instances created after the change. The seed image is written once and never refreshed, so existing instances keep their current configuration.

## Related Issue(s)

None

## Type of Change

- [ ] Bug fix
- [ ] New feature
- [ ] Breaking change
- [ ] Refactor
- [ ] Documentation
- [x] Other (performance)

## Test Plan

Measured on ubuntu:noble with 2 vCPUs, 1G of memory and KVM, timing from `cubic start` until the guest greets on the forwarded SSH port, three runs per configuration.

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| time to SSH greeting, median | 20.97s | 18.48s |
| config-ssh | 1.442s | 0.023s |
| config-resizefs | 0.622s | 0.004s |

Per module numbers come from `cloud-init analyze blame` in the guest.

title: Add templates
body:
## Summary

Adds template support to `cubic create` and `cubic run`. A template is a TOML file holding default values for a new VM instance, so a setup can be written once, reused, and shared instead of retyping a long command line. It covers the image, machine size, forwarded ports and commands that run on the first boot, and every command line argument overrides the matching template value.

```toml
version = 1

image = "debian:trixie"
cpus = 4
memory = "4G"
ports = ["8000:80"]

run = [
  "sudo apt update",
  "sudo apt install -y apache2",
]
```

```
$ cubic create my-instance --template ./my-template.toml
```

This follows the design agreed in the issue thread. The template carries no instance name, so one file can create many machines. `--image` is now optional, since the template can supply it, and `-e/--execute` is repeatable to mirror the template's `run` list. A `--no-isolate` argument was added so a template that sets `isolate = true` can still be overridden from the command line, keeping the override rule true for every field.

The branch also carries a separate fix. The first boot command reached cloud-init as `bootcmd`, which cloud-init runs on every boot, so a package install repeated on each start. It is now passed as `runcmd` and runs once, matching what the flag has always documented.

title: [Feature]: Add latest and stable tags to every distribution
body:
## Feature Description

Give every distribution two extra names, `latest` and `stable`.

`latest` always points at the newest release of a distribution. Development and daily images stay out of it.

`stable` points at the newest long term release. For Ubuntu that is the last LTS and for Debian it is the current stable. For distributions with rolling releases `stable` points at the same image as `latest`. Both names then work everywhere and mean something sensible.

A bare vendor name is a shortcut for `stable`. So `--image ubuntu` gives you the last LTS.

## Use Case

Right now every command needs an exact version or a codename. So `cubic run vm --image ubuntu:noble` has to be edited by hand the moment a new release lands. The same applies to scripts, docs and the README. Everything drifts out of date together.

The two tags remove that chore. Write `ubuntu:latest` for the freshest Ubuntu. Write `ubuntu:stable` or just `ubuntu` for the one with five years of support. Both keep working release after release.

## Proposed Solution

Resolve the tags in the image factory while the image list is built.

Add a method to `ImageProvider` that returns the stable version of a distribution. Each provider knows its own release scheme. Ubuntu picks the newest LTS. Debian picks the current stable. Distributions with rolling releases return the one version they have. The default implementation returns the latest version and gives the fallback behaviour for free.

The tags join `Image.names`. So `cubic images` shows them on the row that already exists and adds no new ones.

ubuntu:{26.04, noble, latest, stable}
ubuntu:{25.10, questing}
arch:{latest, stable}

A tag resolves once when an instance is created. The instance then records the version it resolved to. An instance created today from `ubuntu:latest` stays on `ubuntu:26.04` even after the next release appears.

## Additional Context

This touches almalinux, archlinux, debian, fedora, gentoo, opensuse, rockylinux and ubuntu. The distributions with rolling releases already expose a single `latest` name and only need `stable` added next to it.

title: [Feature]: Add support for temporary instances
body:
## Feature Description

A nameless `cubic run` starts a temporary instance. All writes go to a throwaway overlay instead of the disk image. When the SSH session ends the VM stops and the overlay is discarded. Nothing is persisted and the base image is never modified.

## Use Case

Quick disposable VMs for a one off test or command, with no cleanup and no leftover disks. Today every `cubic run` leaves a named instance behind that the user has to delete by hand.

## Proposed Solution

- `cubic run -i debian:trixie` with no instance name launches a temporary instance from the base image in the cache.
- Start qemu with `-snapshot` so every write lands in a temp file in the host temp directory and qemu drops it on exit.
- SSH attaches as usual. When the session ends, cubic stops the VM, so qemu discards the overlay.
- A guest reboot keeps the overlay because the qemu process stays alive. A full stop discards it.
- Print a clear line such as "Starting a temporary instance, it will be removed when you exit" so the mode is never a surprise.
- The instance is not written to the instance store, so it never appears in `cubic list`.

## Alternatives Considered

- A `--temporary` flag on `create` or `start`. More surface and less discoverable than a nameless `run`.
- Cubic managing its own qcow2 overlay with a backing file and deleting it on stop. Works, but reimplements what qemu `-snapshot` already does.

title: [Feature]: Group subcommands under section headings in --help
body:
## Use Case

The flat list is long and scatters related commands, so a new user has to read
the whole thing to find the few commands they need. Headings make the help
scannable and show at a glance which commands belong together.

## Proposed Solution

clap 4.6 cannot group subcommands, and the upstream issue has been open since
2019 with a stalled PR (clap-rs/clap#1553, clap-rs/clap#6183), so we render the
grouped list ourselves.

- Hide every subcommand with `hide = true` so clap stops printing the flat list.
- Keep a group table in code that maps each subcommand to a heading.
- Build the grouped listing at runtime from `CommandDispatcher::command()`,
  reading `get_name` and `get_about`, styled with the command styles so it keeps
  the current colors.
- Inject the listing through a runtime `help_template` so it stays above
  `Options:` where the command list is today.
- Restore `[COMMAND]` in the usage line with `override_usage`, since hiding all
  subcommands drops it.
- Add a unit test that asserts every subcommand appears in exactly one group, so
  a new command cannot silently fall out of the help.

This uses only public clap API and leaves parsing unchanged. Shell completions
still work because `clap_complete` sees the hidden subcommands.

title: [Feature]: Use the system proxy settings
body:
## Feature Description

Cubic should use the proxy the operating system is configured with when it lists
images and downloads files.

## Use Case

A user on macOS or Windows sets a proxy in the system settings. Browsers and
package managers follow it, cubic does not, so every image list and download
fails with no hint that the proxy is the cause. There is also nothing to copy,
since the address lives in a settings dialog.

On Linux and the BSDs cubic already follows `HTTP_PROXY` and `HTTPS_PROXY`, so
this is about macOS and Windows.

## Proposed Solution

Read the proxy configuration from the operating system on macOS and
Windows and apply it to every request cubic makes.

## Documentation

Add `docs/howto/proxy.rst` and list it in the How-To toctree in
`docs/index.rst`. It should say which proxy settings cubic picks up per platform
and name the limits, so a proxy needing a user name and password and a proxy
configured through a PAC file.

## Alternatives Considered

Exporting `HTTP_PROXY` and `HTTPS_PROXY` by hand in every shell. This works
today and stays useful, but it does not help a user whose proxy is only
system settings.

## Additional Context

All network access goes through `src/web/web_client.rs`, so this should be a
contained change. Cubic pulls in `reqwest` with default features turned off,
which is what switches off the built in operating system proxy detection today.

title: [Feature]: Route all input through a single broker behind the System trait
body:
## Feature Description

Give stdin one owner that sits behind the `System` traits, instead of three readers that each take it on their own. `read_input` and `read_secret` in `src/platform/os_terminal.rs` read stdin directly, and `src/ssh/ssh_client.rs` and `src/commands/console_command.rs` each call `tokio::io::stdin()` inline. The last two bypass the trait layer entirely, so the ssh and console passthrough cannot be tested without a real terminal.

## Use Case

Input becomes mockable like every other host resource, which is how the rest of the codebase is built. The passthrough paths get their first tests, the prompts get tests that do not depend on a tty, and later work on richer input has one seam to grow behind instead of three.

## Proposed Solution

The `Terminal` trait hands out the input stream and nothing more. One method returning `Box<dyn AsyncRead>`, over `tokio::io::stdin()` on `OsSystem` and over a `Cursor` on `SystemMock`, the way `ReadWrite` in `src/platform/read_write.rs` hides a transport. After this nothing outside `os_terminal.rs` names stdin.

The broker sits on top, outside the platform layer, owning one buffer with two views. A line and key view for the prompts, and passthrough for ssh and console, where `ShortcutDecoder` in `src/util/shortcut_decoder.rs` drops in unchanged. It works on bytes rather than crossterm events, since decoded events cannot be turned back into bytes for passthrough.

Most of the decoder already exists. The loop in `read_secret` at `os_terminal.rs:49` to `:85` handles Ctrl+C, CR and LF, backspace and delete, incremental UTF-8 assembly, and EOF, which is the key view minus echo and escape sequences. The work is lifting it one layer up, so keep the partial UTF-8 handling and the rule that a non empty pending buffer at the terminator is an error. What is new is the source, the buffer outliving a single call, and the passthrough view.

`read_input` and `read_secret` then move off the trait onto the broker, so the trait shrinks rather than grows. `read_input` becomes the same loop with echo, and `read_secret` returns an error on Ctrl+C instead of calling `std::process::exit(1)`, which keeps process control out of the platform layer.

One supporting change makes this safe. `AsyncCaller` builds a throwaway `current_thread` runtime per call and shuts it down in the background, so a handle created in one call and polled in the next would strand its buffered bytes. It becomes one shared long lived runtime, with sync prompts driving the broker through `block_on`. `System` stays `Rc` based, so only the stream handle needs to be `Send`. On the mock side `push_input` keeps its signature and feeds the cursor, so existing tests are untouched.

Raw mode stays per command exactly as it is today. Global raw mode, the `\r\n` change in `Console::emit`, the signal handler and the Ctrl+C watch sit on top of this seam and are tracked separately, so the key view lands with tests but without a user visible effect until then.

## Possible Subtasks

1. Turn `AsyncCaller` into one shared long lived runtime, replacing the three throwaway ones in `ssh_client.rs` and `console_command.rs`.
2. Put the input stream on the `Terminal` trait, real on `OsSystem` and a cursor on `SystemMock`.
3. Add the broker, lifting the decode loop out of `read_secret` onto a buffer that outlives a call, tested against byte fixtures.
4. Move the ssh and console passthrough onto the broker, with `ShortcutDecoder` unchanged, and add the first tests for those paths.
5. Move `read_input` and `read_secret` off the trait, add echo to `read_input`, and replace the direct exit with an error return.

title: [Feature]: Redesign the on disk layout around one root and hex ids
body:
## Feature Description

Put everything cubic owns under one root, one flat directory per instance, named by a random hex id instead of by the user's instance name.

## Use Case

**One instance lives in four places.** The config, disk and keys in `~/.local/share/cubic/machines/<name>/`, the cloud-init seed in `~/.cache/cubic/instances/<name>/`, the pid file in `/run/user/<uid>/cubic/instances/<name>/`, and images in a fourth tree. Backup, delete and rename each have to visit all of them, and a rename that fails halfway leaves the instance split across two names.

**The name is the path.** `^[\w_-]+$` with a unicode aware `\w` means `café` is a legal instance name and becomes a directory. macOS folds it, case insensitive volumes collide `Foo` with `foo`, Windows accepts `con`, and nothing caps the length.

**Four things are simply missing.** No lock, so two cubic processes can race. No log, so a VM that fails to boot leaves nothing behind. No creation date. And the QEMU monitor is a loopback TCP port that needs five pem files per instance to make it safe.

## Proposed Solution

One root. `$XDG_DATA_HOME/cubic` on Linux, `~/Library/cubic` on macOS, `%LOCALAPPDATA%\cubic` on Windows, mode `0700`.

```
<root>/
  cubic.lock
  images/<id>/
    image.toml          vendor, name, arch, url, sha256, format
    disk.img
  instances/<id>/
    config.toml         version, name, created_at, created_by, cpus, memory,
                        disk, ssh_port, image id
    lock
    disk.img
    ssh_client_key
    cloud-init.iso
    monitor.sock
    console.sock
    qemu.pid
    serial.log
    qemu.log
```

An id is 64 random bits as 16 hex characters. One instance is one flat directory, so copy, delete and inspect are single operations on a single path.

The directory says which instance you are in, so the file names say what each file is. No name repeats the word instance and no name states a format the file already declares in its own header. A future global config takes `<root>/settings.toml`, so it never collides with the per instance `config.toml`.

| Today | New |
| --- | --- |
| the name is the directory | a hex id is the directory, the name lives in `config.toml` |
| four trees | one root at `0700` |
| monitor and console on `127.0.0.1` plus five pem files | `monitor.sock` and `console.sock` |
| no locking | `cubic.lock` for the tree, `lock` per instance |
| no logs | `serial.log` and `qemu.log`, truncated on start |
| no dates | `created_at` and `created_by` |
| `<name>.tmp` staging directory | write `config.toml` last, a directory without one is incomplete |

`cubic list` gains an ID column and every command accepts a name or a unique id prefix.

### Names

Unique, compared case insensitively, matching `^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,62}$`. Renaming becomes one config write.

ASCII is a deferral, not a verdict. Because the id carries the path, allowing unicode later is a change to the validator alone.

title: refactor: split System into one trait per OS resource
body:
## Summary

`system.rs`, `os_system.rs` and `system_mock.rs` had grown too big to read comfortably. `System` described the whole host in a single trait with every method in one file, and both implementations grew alongside it.

`System` is now split into `FileSystem`, `Process`, `Network`, `Terminal` and `Host`, one trait per OS resource. It stays on as an empty supertrait over the five, so every caller keeps taking `System` and no signature changed. `Process` deliberately keeps `run_command`, `spawn_command`, `exists_process` and `kill_process` together, because a spawn creates the very pid a later kill acts on.

Both implementations follow the same split, so everything about one resource sits in one file. `OsSystem` keeps its struct and nothing else, with its impls in `os_file_system.rs`, `os_process.rs`, `os_network.rs`, `os_terminal.rs` and `os_host.rs`. The mock follows the same shape, each mock struct named after its resource and ending in `Mock`, with the builder methods sitting next to the trait they configure.

This is a pure restructuring. Narrowing callers onto the single traits they use is deliberately left out, since it touches every command and belongs in its own change. Trait upcasting from `&dyn System` works on the pinned toolchain, so each caller can be narrowed later without touching its callers.

Two removals came along with it. Five mock tests that only proved a value could be stored and read back, and the `set_terminal` builder, which no test ever called.

**1. The process id moves behind `--all`.** `cubic show` printed `PID` as the second row and `cubic instances` had a `PID` column. Both are now shown only with `--all`, where the pid joins `Disk Image`, `Config` and `SSH Key` at the bottom.

**2. `cubic show` omits a field instead of printing `n/a`.** This affects `Disk Used`, `Monitor Port` and `Console Port` on an instance, `PID` under `--all`, and `Size` on an image. Since the key column is sized from the longest label present, dropping `Monitor Port` also narrows the block.

before                          after
Running:      no                Running:    no
PID:          n/a               Arch:       amd64
Arch:         amd64             CPUs:       1
CPUs:         1                 Memory:     1.0 GiB
Memory:       1.0 GiB           Disk Total: 2.2 GiB
Disk Used:    n/a               User:       cubic
Disk Total:   2.2 GiB           Isolated:   no
User:         cubic             SSH Port:   14357
Isolated:     no

Monitor Port: n/a
Console Port: n/a
```

It now prints `instance.hostfwd` only. With no rules anywhere you used to get a bare header, so that case now explains itself.

Instance   Host             Guest  Protocol     No port forwarding rules are configured.
noble      127.0.0.1:30612  :22    /tcp         Add one with cubic modify <instance> --port <host_port>:<guest_port>

The function already returns `Option<Image>`, so it now returns `None` and logs the url and the error under `--verbose`.

title: [Feature]: Mount a host directory into a guest machine
body:
## Feature Description

A user names a directory on the host and sees it inside the machine. The directory can
be attached to a running machine and detached again. Changes on either side show up on
the other, and files stay editable on both sides with no permission fixing needed. The
user can see which directories a machine has.

## Use Case

People want to keep their work where it already is. The editor, the files and the git
checkout stay on the host. The build and the risky commands belong in the machine.
Cubic has no way to connect those two sides.

The whole feature is one expectation. A user saves a file on the host and the machine
sees it right away.

## Proposed Solution

Left open. Cubic runs without root and asks the user to install nothing extra. Any
approach has to keep that promise.

Open questions worth settling first.

- Does a shared directory come back after the machine is stopped and started
- Does the user pick where it appears inside the machine, or does cubic pick
- Is read only sharing worth offering, or is read and write enough to start

## Alternatives Considered

Cubic offers `scp` today, which copies files once. That is fine for moving something
across and wrong for working. The copy is out of date as soon as the user types the
next line, and results built in the machine have to be copied back. The two sides
drift, and the user finds out when they build something that is not what they were
looking at.

title: [Feature]: Snapshot and restore a machine
body:
# Feature Description

 Cubic has no way to save what a machine looks like right now and go back to it later.
 It should. A user should be able to name a snapshot of a stopped machine, keep a few of
 them around, and roll the machine back to whichever one they want.

 # Use Case

 Most people run a VM because they are about to break something. They spend a while
 getting the machine into good shape, then run whatever they were actually there to run,
 and it leaves a mess behind. The next run should start from the same clean state, but
 there is no way to get back to it. The machine has to be deleted and built again, so
 the image downloads again and every setup step happens again.

 Clone gets asked about here and it does not solve it. A clone is a second machine with
 its own name, its own ports and its own row in cubic list, and the machine that broke
 is still broken. It also costs a full copy of the disk every time. Snapshots inside a
 qcow2 image share the blocks that never changed, so keeping several of them stays
 cheap.

 One save point per machine would not be enough either. Setup happens in stages, and any
 of them can be the one worth going back to. Somebody might keep a clean state, a
 deps state and a configured state and pick between them.

 This only needs to work on stopped machines. Snapshotting a running machine with its
 memory is a much bigger job and should stay out of this.

# Proposed Solution

 Roughly what a user needs:

 - Create a snapshot of a stopped machine under a name
 - List the snapshots a machine has

title: [Feature]: Re-enable WHPX acceleration on Windows.
body:
## Feature Description

Re-enable the WHPX accelerator on Windows so that VMs get hardware acceleration again instead of falling back to TCG software emulation.

WHPX was disabled in `QemuSystem::get_accelerator` (`src/qemu/qemu_system.rs`) because the accelerator and the CPU model could not be reconciled. Windows currently starts QEMU with `-cpu max -accel tcg`.

## Use Case

WHPX is the only hardware accelerator available on Windows. Without it every instance runs under software emulation, which makes boot and any real workload noticeably slower. Restoring acceleration brings Windows in line with KVM on Linux and HVF on macOS.

## Proposed Solution

The blocker is that `-cpu` is hardcoded to a single value in `QemuSystem::from` and shared by every accelerator.

* WHPX needs `-cpu host`. With the current `-cpu max` the guest hangs at the OVMF firmware screen and never reaches the guest OS, see #500.
* `-cpu host` cannot become the global default because it breaks TCG on the other platforms.

So the CPU model has to be chosen per accelerator rather than once for all of them, `host` when WHPX is selected and `max` for the TCG path.

The second half is a real fallback. Today `-accel tcg` is appended after the platform accelerator on the assumption that QEMU falls through when the first one fails. That assumption does not hold for the hang in #500, because WHPX initialises fine and only then hangs, so QEMU never reaches TCG. Cubic should verify that WHPX is usable on the host before selecting it, and pick TCG with `-cpu max` otherwise.

## Alternatives Considered

* Making `-cpu host` the global default, which breaks TCG everywhere else.
* Leaving WHPX enabled and documenting the hang, which was rejected because the failure mode is a silent hang with no error output.

## Additional Context

Related to #500, where enabling Hyper-V on a Windows host reproduces the hang reliably. Until this is solved, users who want to experiment with WHPX can pass the flags manually.

```
cubic start <instance> --qemu-args "-accel whpx -cpu host"
```

title: [Bug]: VM hangs at OVMF firmware screen on Windows when Hyper-V is enabled"
body:
## Describe the Bug

On Windows, when Hyper-V is activated, cubic VMs get stuck at the OVMF firmware boot process and never reach the guest OS.

## Steps to Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Enable Hyper-V on a Windows host (any Windows version).
2. Run `cubic` to start a VM.
3. VM boots QEMU and hangs at the OVMF firmware boot.

## Expected Behavior

The VM should boot past OVMF and reach the guest OS, same as when Hyper-V is disabled.

## Actual Behavior

The VM hangs indefinitely at the OVMF firmware screen.

## Environment

- **Cubic Version**: affects any version, but first detected in v0.24.1
- **Installation Method**: `winget install cubic-vm.cubic`
- **Operating System**: any Windows version, reproduces whenever Hyper-V is
  activated
- **Architecture**: `amd64`

## Additional Context

Toggling Hyper-V off makes the issue go away, toggling it on reproduces it reliably. This points at the WHPX accelerator path (QEMU's Windows Hypervisor Platform backend, which requires Hyper-V).

The commit message check only allowed feat, fix, refactor, docs, chore, and revert. This was missing common types like ci and test, even though old commits in this repo already used them.

Add perf, style, test, build, and ci to both the check script and the contributing guide, so the full standard set of commit types is now allowed.

title: Test Suite Clean up
body:
## Summary

This cleans up the test suite. It fixes broken tests, removes flaky and duplicate tests, and adds coverage for parts of the code that had none.

## Changes

* Fixed broken assertions and misleading test names
* Made `QemuPathBuilder` testable by injecting the directory list instead of reading the environment
* Removed tests that depended on the host environment or repeated the same check
* Added tests for error paths in parsers and models
* Added tests for image provider parsing
* Added tests for port listing and command guards
* Made test mocks more flexible so more code paths can be tested

title: Route terminal prompts through Console and fix SSH password entry bugs
body:
## Description

### Summary

- Routes confirm() prompts and SSH password entry through `Console` instead of talking to stdin/stdout directly, so both share the same animation-muting logic and can be exercised through `ConsoleMock` in tests.
- Fixes a bug where the "Authenticating on {machine}" spinner kept rendering over the SSH password prompt during entry.
- Fixes several correctness bugs in the password-reading loop that came along for the ride: invalid UTF-8 silently became an empty password, backspace removed a raw byte instead of a full character, `~` was misread as backspace, and a closed stdin spun forever instead of erroring out.
- Shows the instance name instead of a hardcoded "localhost" in the SSH password prompt.
- Replaces the `confirm()` free function with a `ConfirmDialog` view struct, matching the rest of the codebase's view conventions, and widens accepted replies to `y`/`yes` case-insensitively.

### Commits

- `refactor: read confirm() input through Console instead of stdin`
  Adds `Console::prompt()` so `confirm()` reads through `Console` rather than raw stdin, and mutes the spinner while a prompt is up.
- `fix: read SSH password prompts through Console instead of raw stdio`
  Adds `Console::prompt_password()`, reusing the same mute/unmute mechanism, and fixes the UTF-8/backspace/EOF/panic bugs in the old raw byte-reading loop.
- `fix: show the instance name in the SSH password prompt`
  Shows the instance name instead of "localhost" in the password prompt text.
- `refactor: turn confirm() into a ConfirmDialog view`
  Replaces the `confirm()` free function with a `ConfirmDialog` view struct owning the `[y/N]` hint and case-insensitive accept logic.

title: fix: disable raw mode on panic
body:
Install a panic hook in main() that disables raw mode on panic.

Fixes #444

title: Small Clean ups
body:
### Summary

This PR is a pure idiom cleanup pass across the codebase, no intended behavior change, split into thirteen focused commits so each intent lands on its own and can be reviewed or bisected independently.

Covers: `Protocol`/`Arch` gaining `Copy` and `Eq`, `Target` display and tilde expansion rewritten without regex, lazy `_else` fallback conversions, a new `format_or_na` helper deduping "n/a" rendering, `InstanceStore::get_pid` returning `Option` instead of a meaningless unit `Result`, TOML deserializer and instance listing plumbing simplified to `Option` combinators, and `create_dir` dropping a racy exists check.

title: fix: stop unknown images from silently resolving to almalinux
body: When cubic create received an unknown image while the local cache had expired, it silently downloaded almalinux instead of reporting an error. The fallback path returned the entire stale cache and picked the first entry regardless of the request. The fix applies the requested filter to that fallback path as well, producing a clear error for an unknown image and the correct download otherwise.

title: fix: make cubic report failure to the shell
body:
Cubic always exited with a success status, even when a command failed. Callers had no reliable way to detect failures, which is a problem for scripts and CI pipelines that check the exit code.

Cubic now exits with a non zero status whenever a command fails.

Fixes #441

title: chore: lock cargo commands in pull request workflow
body:
Run clippy, test, build and run with --locked so a stale or dirty Cargo.lock fails on the pull request instead of only surfacing at release time.

Fixes #465

title: fix: enable ANSI virtual terminal processing on Windows
body:
Windows printed raw escape codes instead of colors and cursor movement from the guest SSH shell. The console never had ANSI virtual terminal processing turned on for its output.

This change turns on ANSI support on Windows when the console starts up. Other platforms are unaffected.

title: Document Windows winget Installation
body: Cubic is now installable on Windows via winget, which pulls in QEMU automatically as a dependency. Document it in the README, the project website install grid, and the install how-to guide, placed between Homebrew and Cargo to match the recommended path.

title: Verbose debug logging and SSH connection spinners
body:
## Summary

Add `--verbose` diagnostics to help users troubleshoot stuck or failing commands, and show progress during SSH connections.

- Add `console.debug()`, a green, `--verbose`-gated output level on the `Console` trait
- Wire debug output into resolved instance settings, SSH port and memory-fit decisions, the SSH auth fallback chain, QEMU firmware discovery, and image list fetching
- Move the QEMU command line print (previously its own verbose flag) onto the same `console.debug()` path
- Remove `Console::get_verbosity()`, left unused by this change
- Add spinners for the connecting, authenticating, and shell setup phases of an SSH session
- Stop the authenticating spinner immediately when `authenticate()` returns, keeping it cleared after a failed login

title: fix: validate instance name arguments against path traversal
body:
Instance names were passed as raw strings and joined onto the machines directory, so names like ../../../dir escaped it. Parse all instance name arguments into the validated InstanceName type via new reusable clap arg structs, reject empty name lists, and add tests.

Fixes #440

title: [Feature]: Lint shell scripts with shellcheck
body:
## Feature Description

Add a shellcheck step so the project's shell scripts are linted the same way the YAML
files already are.

## Use Case

The lint job runs `yamllint --strict`, but the shell scripts that drive commit
validation and the documentation build are not checked at all. These scripts use
`set -euo pipefail` and some subtle quoting, so a small mistake can pass review and
break a release or a required check.

## Proposed Solution

Add a `shellcheck` step to the existing lint job that covers `check-pr-commits.sh`,
`generate-docs.sh` and `generate-page.sh`. Fix or annotate any findings so the check
starts green.

## Additional Context

- `.github/workflows/pull-request.yml` lint job currently runs only yamllint
- `.github/scripts/check-pr-commits.sh`, `scripts/generate-docs.sh`,
  `scripts/generate-page.sh`

title: [Feature]: Add concurrency cancellation and job timeouts to the workflows
body:
## Feature Description

Give the workflows a concurrency group that cancels superseded runs and a timeout on
each job so a stuck step cannot run for hours.

## Use Case

Neither workflow sets a `concurrency` group, so pushing several times to a pull request
or to main leaves redundant full runs queued and running. No job sets `timeout-minutes`,
so a hung network step or a stuck build can occupy a runner for the default six hours,
which wastes minutes and delays feedback.

## Proposed Solution

Add a concurrency group keyed on the workflow and the ref with cancel in progress
enabled for pull requests, and set a sensible `timeout-minutes` on each job. Leave the
release and publish jobs without cancellation so a tag build is never interrupted.

## Additional Context

- `.github/workflows/pull-request.yml` and `.github/workflows/build.yml`
- The publish-doc job already uses a pages concurrency group that should stay as is

title: [Feature]: Run cargo audit on a schedule instead of a hard gate on every PR
body:
## Feature Description

Move the security advisory check off the critical path of every pull request so a new
advisory does not block unrelated work.

## Use Case

The pull request workflow installs cargo-audit and runs `cargo audit` as a required
check. Advisories are published continuously, so a pull request that never touched the
dependencies can start failing the day a new advisory lands. That makes the check time
dependent and blocks contributors for reasons outside their change.

## Proposed Solution

Run the audit in a scheduled job, for example daily, with a dedicated workflow or the
`rustsec/audit-check` action, and keep the existing suppression flow in
`.cargo/audit.toml` and `vulnlog.yml`. A lighter audit can still run on pull requests,
but the deterministic checks should be the ones that gate a merge.

## Additional Context

- `.github/workflows/pull-request.yml` check matrix runs `cargo install cargo-audit`
  then `cargo audit`
- `.cargo/audit.toml` and `vulnlog.yml` already track accepted advisories

title: [Feature]: Cache Rust builds and tool installs in CI
body:
## Feature Description

Add build and tool caching to the CI workflows so jobs stop recompiling everything from
scratch on every run.

## Use Case

Neither workflow caches the cargo registry or the target directory, and the audit and
deb jobs run `cargo install cargo-audit` and `cargo install cargo-deb`, which compile
those tools every time. The result is slow feedback on pull requests and wasted runner
minutes on releases.

## Proposed Solution

Add a Rust cache such as `Swatinem/rust-cache` to the build, check and test jobs, and
install the toolchain with `--profile minimal` so setup skips components that are not
needed. Cache or pin the helper tools so cargo-audit and cargo-deb are not rebuilt each
run.

## Additional Context

- `.github/workflows/pull-request.yml` check and build jobs
- `.github/workflows/build.yml` build, package-deb and validate jobs

title: [Bug]: The Docker build image installs genisoimage, which is unused
body:
## Describe the Bug

The build image installs `genisoimage`, but cubic no longer shells out to it. The
cloud-init seed is now built by a pure Rust writer, so the package is dead weight in the
image and misleads a reader into thinking it is a runtime requirement.

## Where

- `Dockerfile` apt install list includes `genisoimage`
- `src/cloudinit/user_data_image_factory.rs` builds the seed with
  `UserDataImageFactory::create_rust`, which calls `iso_writer.create_iso`
- A search of `src` finds no genisoimage invocation

## Impact

The build image is larger than it needs to be and the dependency list no longer
reflects what cubic actually uses.

## Suggested Fix

Remove `genisoimage` from the Dockerfile. While there, consider copying the cargo
manifests before the full source so a source edit does not rebuild the apt and cargo
layers, which speeds up local image rebuilds.

title: [Bug]: Unit tests run only on Linux although three OSes are built
body:
## Describe the Bug

The pull request workflow runs `cargo test` only on Linux. The check matrix that holds
the test step uses `ubuntu-latest` alone, and the separate build matrix that does run on
Linux, macOS and Windows only builds and prints help, never running the tests. Cross
platform behavior is therefore never unit tested on macOS or Windows.

## Where

- `.github/workflows/pull-request.yml` check matrix runs `cargo test` on `ubuntu-latest`
- `.github/workflows/pull-request.yml` build matrix on ubuntu, macos and windows runs
  only `cargo build` and `cargo run -- --help`

## Impact

The path handling, environment lookup and firmware discovery differ per operating
system, and cubic supports all three as hosts. A regression that only shows up on macOS
or Windows would pass CI unnoticed.

## Suggested Fix

Run `cargo test` on all three runners, either by adding the test step to the three OS
build matrix or by expanding the check matrix to cover macOS and Windows.

title: [Bug]: Pull request build and test do not use --locked
body:
## Describe the Bug

The pull request checks build and test without `--locked`, so a stale or dirty
`Cargo.lock` passes review. Cargo silently updates the lock file when it is out of
sync, which hides the drift. The release build uses `cargo build --locked --release`,
so the mismatch only surfaces when a tag is cut.

## Where

- `.github/workflows/pull-request.yml` runs `cargo build` and `cargo test` with no
  `--locked`
- `.github/workflows/build.yml` build job uses `cargo build --locked --release`

## Impact

A pull request can pass every check and then break the release build because the lock
file does not match `Cargo.toml`. The failure appears at release time, far from the
change that caused it.

## Suggested Fix

Add `--locked` to the build and test commands in the pull request workflow so lock file
drift fails on the pull request instead of at release.

title: [Bug]: Release binaries and the deb package report version 0.0.0-dev
body:
## Describe the Bug

The build job compiles the release binaries while `Cargo.toml` still carries
`version = "0.0.0-dev"`. The release and deb jobs reuse those artifacts, so the
published binaries and the deb report `0.0.0-dev` from `cubic --version`. Only the
crate publish patches the version, and only the snap sets its own version, so the
version a user sees depends on how they installed cubic.

## Where

- `.github/workflows/build.yml` build job compiles without patching the version
- `.github/workflows/build.yml` publish-release reuses the build artifacts
- `.github/workflows/build.yml` package-deb builds from the unpatched manifest
- publish-crate patches the version with sed and package-snap overrides it separately

## Impact

A released binary and the deb both answer `0.0.0-dev` to `--version`, which makes bug
reports harder and disagrees with the crate and snap versions.

## Suggested Fix

Stamp the version once, early, before the build job compiles, derived from the tag, so
every artifact carries the same version. Then the release, deb, crate and snap agree.

title: [Feature]: Add a how-to for installing shell completions
body:
## Feature Description

Add a short how-to that shows how to generate and install shell completion scripts with
the `completions` command.

## Use Case

Cubic ships a `completions` command and it has a reference page, but there is no guide
that shows how to turn its output into working tab completion for a shell. Users who
would benefit most from completions are unlikely to find the feature from the reference
page alone.

## Proposed Solution

Add a page under `docs/howto/` that shows generating the script for bash, zsh and fish
and where to place or source it for each shell. Link it from the site index next to the
other how-to guides.

## Additional Context

- `docs/reference/completions.rst` documents the command itself
- `src/commands/completions_command.rs` is the implementation behind it

title: [Feature]: Add a troubleshooting page for QEMU and firmware not found
body:
## Feature Description

Add a troubleshooting page that maps the most common first run failure, a missing QEMU
or UEFI firmware, to the steps that fix it.

## Use Case

When QEMU or the firmware is not present, cubic stops with a QEMU not found error. The
QEMU detection page explains where cubic searches, but nothing connects the visible
error to a fix, so a new user has to infer it. A short troubleshooting entry would turn
a dead end into a clear next step.

## Proposed Solution

Add a page under `docs/troubleshooting/` that names the error, shows how to install
QEMU and the firmware (OVMF for amd64 and AAVMF or edk2 for arm64) per platform, and
points at `CUBIC_QEMU_DIR` and the `CUBIC_QEMU_FW_*` variables for non standard
locations. Link it from the site index. While in the recovery guide, add a note that
the snap package strips `qemu-nbd`, so snap users need their distribution's
`qemu-utils` for the block device method.

## Additional Context

- `docs/internals/qemu_detection.rst` already documents the search order to link to
- `docs/troubleshooting/recover_disk.rst` is where the `qemu-nbd` note belongs

title: [Feature]: Clarify the environment variables how-to and collect the CUBIC variables
body:
## Feature Description

Make the documentation about environment variables clear about which kind it means,
and give cubic's own `CUBIC_*` variables a single reference.

## Use Case

The how-to titled Environment Variables is actually about forwarding host environment
variables into the guest with the `--env` flag. Cubic's own configuration variables,
`CUBIC_QEMU_DIR`, `CUBIC_QEMU_FW_AMD64` and `CUBIC_QEMU_FW_ARM64`, are documented only
on the QEMU detection page. A reader who opens the environment variables page to learn
how to point cubic at a QEMU install finds a different topic and can miss the settings
they need.

## Proposed Solution

Retitle the how-to so it names the `--env` guest passthrough it describes. Add a short
consolidated list of cubic's `CUBIC_*` variables, or cross-link the QEMU detection page
from the how-to so both kinds are easy to find. There is no `CUBIC_QEMU_IMG` variable
in the code, so the list should not include one.

## Additional Context

- `docs/howto/environment_variables.rst` is the guest passthrough guide
- `docs/internals/qemu_detection.rst` holds the current `CUBIC_*` reference

title: [Bug]: rST title underlines are too short and warn on every docs build
body:
## Describe the Problem

Two places in the docs emit reStructuredText title underlines that are shorter than
the title text. Sphinx treats a short underline as a warning on every build, which
adds noise and can hide real problems. One source is the reference generator, which
writes a fixed five character underline under every command title, so all twenty
generated reference pages warn. The other is the install page, where several numbered
section headings have underlines shorter than the heading.

## Where

- `scripts/generate-docs.sh` line 15 writes `$name` followed by a fixed `=====`
- `docs/reference/*.rst` inherit that short underline (for example `cubic create` over
  five equals signs)
- `docs/howto/install.rst` numbered section underlines such as the ones under Install
  Dependencies, Install Rust toolchain, Install Cubic, Update PATH and Test Cubic

## Suggested Fix

Change the generator to write an underline as long as the title, for example by
repeating the underline character to the length of the name, then regenerate the
reference pages so the committed copies are refreshed. Lengthen the install page
section underlines to match their headings. The intent is a docs build with no title
underline warnings.

## Note

The reference pages are generated output, so they should be refreshed by rerunning
`scripts/generate-docs.sh` rather than edited by hand.

title: [Bug]: CONTRIBUTING says use raw cargo while the project builds through make
body:
## Describe the Problem

The contributing guide tells contributors to build, test, format, lint and audit by
calling cargo directly. The project actually builds and tests through the Docker based
make targets, which run those cargo commands inside a pinned container. A contributor
who follows the guide uses a different toolchain than the one the maintainers and CI
use, which can hide formatting and lint differences and version specific failures.

## Where

- `CONTRIBUTING.md` build, test, format, lint and audit sections
- `Makefile` targets `test`, `check`, `fix`, `format`, `lint`, `audit`

## What Is Correct

The intended workflow is `make test`, `make check` and `make fix`, which wrap cargo in
the container defined by the `Makefile`.

## Suggested Fix

Point the contributing guide at the make targets as the primary path. If the raw cargo
commands are still worth showing, mark them as an alternative and state that CI uses the

title: [Bug]: Windows is documented as both native Hyper-V and Snap in WSL
body:
## Describe the Problem

The install page recommends installing on Windows with Snap inside WSL, while the How
Cubic Works page, the site index and the README describe native Windows with hardware
acceleration. These are two different setups. Snap in WSL runs a Linux build that uses
KVM, and native Windows runs the Windows build. A new Windows user cannot tell which
path the project actually intends. The acceleration name is also off, since the Windows
build uses WHPX, the Windows Hypervisor Platform, rather than classic Hyper-V.

## Where

- `docs/howto/install.rst` lines 23 to 30
- `docs/internals/how_it_works.rst` and `docs/index.rst` and `README.md` Windows claims

## What Is Correct

`src/qemu/qemu_system.rs` selects `whpx` on Windows. Native Windows is installed with
Cargo, and the WSL route is a Linux install with Snap and KVM.

## Suggested Fix

Separate the two Windows paths in the docs. Present native Windows with the Cargo
install and WHPX acceleration, and present the WSL route as a Linux install with Snap
and KVM. Correct the accelerator name from Hyper-V to WHPX where the runtime is
described.

title: [Bug]: Getting Started examples are inaccurate and drift prone
body:
## Describe the Problem

The Getting Started page has three example problems. The instance listing sample shows
the machine as running before the guide has started it, and a running machine would
also show a process id, so the sample state is impossible at that point. The create
example uses the `--mem` alias and a double space where the rest of the docs use
`--memory`. The images listing is a large fixed snapshot of every distribution and
version, which will drift as providers change.

## Where

- `docs/howto/getting_started.rst` lines 15 to 48 (images snapshot)
- `docs/howto/getting_started.rst` lines 66 to 68 (running state)
- `docs/howto/getting_started.rst` line 78 (`--mem` and double space)

## What Is Correct

A freshly created machine that has not been started reports Running as no and an empty
process id, which matches `src/commands/show_instance_command.rs` and
`src/commands/list_instance_command.rs`. The canonical flag is `--memory`, with `--mem`
only an alias.

## Suggested Fix

Show the listing with Running as no before the start step, switch the create example to
`--memory` and remove the double space, and trim the images block to a short excerpt
with a note that the full list comes from `cubic images`.

title: [Bug]: The show --all example prints Status and misorders the forward line
body:
## Describe the Problem

The HTTP server how-to shows a `cubic show --all` sample whose first line reads
`Status` with a value of stopped, and it places the forward line after the SSH line.
The real command prints the first field as `Running` with a yes or no value, and it
prints the forward rows before the extra fields that `--all` adds. A reader comparing
their real output to the guide will see different labels and ordering.

## Where

- `docs/howto/http_server.rst` lines 62 to 79

## What Is Correct

`src/commands/show_instance_command.rs` builds the view in this order. Running, PID,
Arch, CPUs, Memory, Disk Used, Disk Total, User, Isolated, SSH Port, Monitor Port,
Console Port, then the forward rows, and only with `--all` the Disk Image, Config, SSH
Key and SSH rows at the end. The unit tests in that file assert exactly this layout,
including the first field named `Running`.

## Suggested Fix

Update the sample block so the first field is `Running` with a yes or no value and the
forward row appears before the Disk Image, Config, SSH Key and SSH rows.

title: [Bug]: How Cubic Works calls the cloud-init seed a CD-ROM but it is a virtio disk
body:
## Describe the Problem

The How Cubic Works page says QEMU mounts the cloud-init ISO as a virtual CD-ROM
drive. The tool no longer does that. The seed is attached as a raw virtio disk, and
QEMU is started with no emulated default devices, so there is no CD-ROM in the
machine at all. The content is still an ISO 9660 filesystem, only the way it is
attached changed.

## Where

- `docs/internals/how_it_works.rst` lines 17 to 18 and 44 to 48

## What Is Correct

`start_instance_action.rs` attaches the seed with `add_drive(user_data_image, "raw")`,
which produces an `if=virtio,format=raw,file=...` drive, and `qemu_system.rs` passes
`-nodefaults`. So cloud-init reads the seed from a small virtio disk on first boot.

## Suggested Fix

Reword the two passages to say a small virtio disk rather than a virtual CD-ROM, and
keep the note that the format is an ISO 9660 filesystem.

title: [Feature]: Build and test on macOS in continuous integration
body:
## Feature Description

Add a macOS job to the build workflow so the supported macOS host is actually built
and tested on every change.

## Use Case

The README lists macOS as a supported host and the code carries a macOS accelerator
path, yet the CI workflow builds only Linux and Windows targets. Nothing catches a
macOS specific break before release, so regressions can ship to macOS users
unnoticed.

## Proposed Solution

Add a macOS runner to `.github/workflows/build.yml` that builds and runs the tests,
including an Apple Silicon target so arm64 macOS is covered. Keep the existing
`cubic --help` smoke check on that runner too.

## Additional Context

The workflow today builds x86_64 Linux, aarch64 Linux and x86_64 Windows.

title: [Feature]: Add machine readable output for the list and show commands
body:
## Feature Description

Offer a machine readable output mode, such as `--json`, for the commands that list
and show instances, images and ports.

## Use Case

The list and show commands render only human tables, so scripting around cubic means
parsing aligned columns that can shift as content changes. A stable JSON form lets
users build tooling on top of cubic without scraping the table layout.

## Proposed Solution

Add an opt in flag that switches the affected commands to emit JSON instead of a
table. The table rendering lives in `src/view/table_view.rs` and
`src/view/map_view.rs`, so a shared path can back both the human and JSON forms.

## Additional Context

Commands in scope are instances, images, ports and the show variants.

title: [Feature]: Give commands consistent success feedback through the console
body:
## Feature Description

Make every mutating command report what it did through the console, so the user gets
the same kind of confirmation whether they create, modify, rename or delete.

## Use Case

Create, delete and prune print what happened, but modify and rename finish in
silence, so the user cannot tell the change landed. Rename does not even take the
console, its handler names the argument `_console`. Delete prints its line with
`println!`, which skips the console and ignores the quiet flag, so it behaves
differently from the rest.

## Proposed Solution

Add a short confirmation line to modify and rename through the console. Change the
delete line to go through the console so `-q` and `-v` are honored like everywhere
else. Keep the wording plain and consistent across commands.

## Additional Context

- `src/commands/modify_command.rs` and `src/commands/rename_command.rs` print nothing
  on success
- `src/commands/delete_command.rs` line 63 uses `println!` instead of the console

title: [Feature]: Make confirmation prompts consistent and accept common yes answers
body:
## Feature Description

Give cubic one confirmation helper that accepts the common yes answers and uses a
single prompt style across every command that asks before acting.

## Use Case

Today the confirm helper treats only a lowercase `y` as yes, so `Y` and `yes` are
read as no. The prompts also differ, with delete showing `[y/n]`, prune showing
`[y/N]` and start showing `[y/n]`, even though all three default to no. Users who
type a natural `Yes` end up cancelling an action they meant to confirm, and the
mixed hints make the real default unclear.

## Proposed Solution

Accept `y` and `yes` in any case as yes, keep everything else as no, and settle on
one prompt style that shows the real default. Route the prompt through the console so
it fits the rest of the output.

## Additional Context

The current helper is `confirm` in `src/util/input.rs` at line 9. The call sites are
the delete, prune and start commands.

title: [Bug]: Data size parsing panics on some inputs and overflows on large values
body:
## Describe the Bug

The data size parser reads the last byte of the input and slices everything before it
by byte index. When the input ends in a multibyte character the slice falls inside
the character and the program panics. Separately the size multiply can overflow the
platform integer on very large inputs and wrap to a wrong value in release builds.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Pass a size that ends in a multibyte character, for example
   `cubic create demo --disk 10€ -i ubuntu:noble`, and watch it panic instead of
   returning a clean parse error
2. Pass a huge size such as a very long number followed by `T` and see the byte count
   wrap to a small wrong number in a release build

## Impact

A user typo can crash the tool instead of producing a friendly message, and an
extreme value can be accepted as a much smaller size than intended.

## Affected Code

- `src/models/data_size.rs` line 41 takes the last byte and slices `value[..len-1]`
- `src/models/data_size.rs` line 53 multiplies without an overflow check

## Suggested Fix

Split on a character boundary rather than a byte index, and use a checked multiply
that returns the normal parse error on overflow. The existing error message already
fits both cases.

## Environment

Applies to the main branch on all supported host platforms.

title: [Bug]: The qemu-args option is split on spaces and breaks quoted arguments
body:
## Describe the Bug

The passthrough for extra QEMU arguments splits the string on a single space. Any
argument that legitimately contains a space is torn into pieces, so quoting on the
command line does not survive.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start with an extra argument that contains a space, for example
   `cubic start my-instance --qemu-args "-chardev socket,path=/tmp/a b"`
2. Observe QEMU receiving `/tmp/a` and `b` as separate tokens
3. See QEMU reject the mangled option

## Impact

Users cannot pass any QEMU option whose value contains a space, which quietly limits
the escape hatch the flag is meant to provide and produces confusing QEMU errors.

## Affected Code

- `src/qemu/qemu_system.rs` line 154 `set_qemu_args` splits on a single space

## Suggested Fix

Parse the string with a shell word splitter so quotes and escapes are honored, or
document clearly that each call passes exactly one token and expect the user to
repeat the flag for more.

## Environment

Applies to the main branch on all supported host platforms.

title: [Bug]: Usernames are not validated before reaching cloud-init and SSH
body:
## Describe the Bug

The create command takes the user name as a raw string with no validation. It is
placed straight into the cloud-init user data without escaping. The user part of an
ssh or scp target is also unvalidated before it is handed to the SSH client.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run create with an odd user name, for example
   `cubic create demo --user "bad name" -i ubuntu:noble`
2. Start the instance and watch cloud-init fail to create the account because the
   generated YAML is malformed
3. Log in and see the expected user is missing

## Impact

A name that contains a space, a newline or a YAML special character breaks
provisioning, and the VM comes up without the account the user asked for. The value
crosses into generated YAML and into an ssh login, so it should be constrained.

## Affected Code

- `src/commands/create_command.rs` line 52 the `user` field is a raw `String`
- `src/cloudinit/user_data_factory.rs` line 24 interpolates the user name without
  escaping
- `src/models/target.rs` line 38 accepts an arbitrary user before ssh

## Suggested Fix

Validate user names with a conservative regex such as `^[a-z_][a-z0-9_-]*$`, close to
the rules real systems use for account names. Apply the same check at the create
boundary and in the target parser so bad input is rejected early.

## Environment

Applies to the main branch on all supported host platforms.

title: [Bug]: A corrupt or missing instance config silently loads as a tiny default
body:
## Describe the Bug

When the loader cannot read or parse an instance config it returns a synthesized
default instance with one vCPU, one gigabyte of memory, one gigabyte of disk and a
fresh SSH port. The yaml to toml migration during load also swallows write errors.
Both cases hide a real problem behind a made up instance.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Corrupt the `instance.toml` of an existing instance, or interrupt a create so the
   directory exists without a config
2. Run a command that loads it such as `cubic show my-instance`
3. See a one vCPU one gigabyte machine reported instead of an error about the broken
   config

## Impact

A user can silently lose the real CPU, memory, disk and port settings and act on a
machine that does not match what they created. A failed migration goes unreported,
so the loss is easy to miss.

## Affected Code

- `src/instance/instance_dao.rs` `load` at line 88 falls back to a default instance
- `src/instance/instance_dao.rs` line 111 migration uses `.ok()` and drops write
  errors

## Suggested Fix

Return an error when a config exists but cannot be read or parsed, so the user
learns the config is broken. Surface a failed migration instead of dropping it. Keep
the default only for the genuine case of no config at all if that path is still
wanted.

## Environment

Applies to the main branch on all supported host platforms.

title: [Bug]: The guest SSH host key is accepted without any verification
body:
## Describe the Bug

The SSH client handler implements the host key check as an unconditional accept.
Cubic never records the guest key on first connect and never compares it on later
connects, so it cannot detect when the key changes.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Connect once with `cubic ssh my-instance`
2. Arrange for a different process to answer on the forwarded loopback port
3. Connect again and see that cubic still accepts the session without any warning

## Impact

Because the forwarded port is on loopback this is not a network man in the middle,
so the severity is limited. Even so, cubic gives up the one protection SSH host keys
provide, which is noticing when the host behind the port has changed. A local
process that grabs the port could impersonate the VM unnoticed.

## Affected Code

- `src/ssh_cmd/russh.rs` line 127 implements `check_server_key` as `Ok(true)`

## Suggested Fix

Pin the guest key on first connect by storing it in the instance directory, then
compare on later connects and warn or refuse when it changes. This mirrors how a
normal SSH client uses a known hosts file.

## Environment

Applies to the main branch on all supported host platforms.

title: [Bug]: A panic during an interactive session leaves the terminal in raw mode
body:
## Describe the Bug

The console output type turns raw mode on and off through explicit calls. Its `Drop`
only stops the animation thread and never disables raw mode. The release profile
builds with panic set to abort, so a panic does not unwind and would not run
destructors anyway. A panic while an ssh or console session holds raw mode leaves
the terminal broken after cubic exits.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start an interactive session such as `cubic ssh my-instance`
2. Trigger a panic in that path
3. After cubic exits, notice the shell no longer echoes input and needs a manual
   `reset`

## Impact

A crash during the most interactive part of the tool leaves the user with an
unusable terminal until they blindly type `reset`. This is exactly when a clean
restore matters most.

## Affected Code

- `src/view/stdio.rs` `Drop for Stdio` at line 228 never calls `disable_raw_mode`
- `Cargo.toml` release profile sets `panic = 'abort'`

## Suggested Fix

Install a panic hook that disables raw mode before the default hook runs, so the
terminal is restored on the way out even under abort. Holding raw mode inside a
guard that the interactive paths own is another option.

## Environment

Applies to the main branch on all supported host platforms. Most visible in release
builds because of the abort setting.

title: [Bug]: Private keys and certificates are written world readable
body:
## Describe the Bug

The per instance certificate generator and the SSH key generator write private key
material with the process umask and never restrict the mode. On a common umask the
files end up readable by other local users.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. On a Linux host create and start an instance so the keys are generated
2. List the instance directory under the data path, for example
   `ls -l ~/.local/share/cubic/machines/<name>`
3. See the private keys and the client key with group and other read bits set

## Impact

On a shared host another local user can read the SSH client key and the QEMU client
certificate and key. With those they can log into the VM and reach the QEMU control
channel that is otherwise protected by mutual TLS.

## Affected Code

- `src/instance/instance_cert_generator.rs` line 50 writes the CA, server and client
  certs and keys with `fs::write`
- `src/ssh_cmd/ssh_key_generator.rs` line 18 writes the SSH private key
- `src/fs.rs` `create_file` opens files without a restricted mode

## Suggested Fix

Create the private key and certificate files with owner only permission. On unix set
the mode to 0o600 when opening, and tighten the instance directory to 0o700. A small
cross platform helper that sets the mode after creation keeps the call sites simple.

## Environment

Applies to the main branch. The permission gap is on unix hosts.

Suggested labels bug, security

title: [Bug]: The console command waits forever when the port never opens
body:
## Describe the Bug

The console command starts the instance without waiting and then loops on a
blocking TCP connect until it succeeds. There is no deadline, so when QEMU never
opens the console port the loop spins with a one second sleep and never returns.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Put the host in a state where the instance cannot open its console port, for
   example by starving memory so QEMU exits early
2. Run `cubic console my-instance`
3. Observe that the command hangs with no timeout and no error

## Impact

The user is stuck with a command that cannot finish and has to kill it by hand. Any
script that opens a console can block forever.

## Affected Code

- `src/commands/console_command.rs` line 52 loops `while TcpStream::connect(...).is_err()`
  with no deadline

## Suggested Fix

Bound the wait the same way the start command already does at
`src/commands/start_command.rs` line 79, which uses a 300 second deadline and
returns `Error::StartTimeout`. Reuse that pattern so console fails cleanly when the
port never opens.

## Environment

Applies to the main branch on all supported host platforms.

title: [Bug]: Cubic exits with code 0 even when a command fails
body:
## Describe the Bug

The entry point maps a failed command to an error print and then calls `.ok()`,
which drops the result. Nothing sets a non zero exit status, so cubic always
returns success to the shell even when the command failed.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run a command that must fail, for example `cubic start does-not-exist`
2. Watch cubic print an error line
3. Run `echo $?` and see 0 instead of a non zero code

## Impact

Scripts, Makefiles and CI pipelines that check the exit status cannot tell that
cubic failed. A failed create or start looks like success, so automation keeps
going as if a VM exists when it never got made.

## Affected Code

- `src/main.rs` line 26 ends the dispatch chain with `.ok()`

## Suggested Fix

When `dispatch` returns an error, print it and exit with a non zero status. One way
is to keep the error print and then call `std::process::exit(1)`. Another is to
return a `std::process::ExitCode` from main and map the error to a failure code.

## Environment

Applies to the main branch on all supported host platforms.

title: [Bug]: Instance name arguments are not validated and allow path traversal
body:
## Describe the Bug

Several commands take the instance name as a raw string and never run it through
the `InstanceName` validation that `create`, `clone` and `rename` use. The name
flows into `Environment::get_instance_dir2`, which joins it onto the machines
directory with `Path::join`. A name that contains a parent reference or an absolute
path escapes the machines directory, so file and directory operations land wherever
the name points.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create any instance so the data directory exists
2. Run `cubic delete ../../../some/writable/dir` with a path that exists
3. Observe that cubic removes that directory instead of rejecting the name

## Impact

`cubic delete` can remove arbitrary directories the user can write to. `cubic
console`, `modify`, `start`, `stop` and `restart` read or act on paths outside the
machines directory in the same way. The name is attacker influenced whenever cubic
is scripted around untrusted input, so this is a local security issue.

## Affected Code

- `src/commands/delete_command.rs` field `instances` is `Vec<String>`
- `src/commands/console_command.rs` field `instance` is `String`
- `src/commands/modify_command.rs` field `instance` is `String`
- `src/commands/start_command.rs`, `stop_command.rs`, `restart_command.rs`
- `src/models/environment.rs` `get_instance_dir2` joins the raw name

## Suggested Fix

Type these fields as `InstanceName` and `Vec<InstanceName>` so clap rejects
traversal input at the boundary. The regex in `src/models/instance_name.rs` already
forbids slashes and dots. A full plan already exists in `InputValidationPlan.md`.

## Environment

Applies to the main branch on all supported host platforms.

Color is skipped when NO_COLOR is set or the stream isn't a real terminal, and is enabled on Windows consoles at startup. Only info is suppressed under quiet mode, warn and error always show.

title: Rework console progress animations to be width-aware
body:
## Summary

Split the console animation refactor into three focused commits:

1. **`refactor: drive console progress through a shared animation loop`**
   Replaces the per-widget `SpinnerView` thread with a single console render loop driven by an `Animation` trait. `Spinner` and `TransferView` implement `Animation` and are played/stopped through the console, which owns one background thread for all progress output. Frames draw only on an interactive TTY and stay silent under `--quiet`.

2. **`refactor: render animations against terminal width`**
   Gives `Animation::render` the current terminal width so `Spinner` and `TransferView` lay text out on the left and status on the right instead of using a fixed-width format. `TransferView` keeps its message in a fixed column and sizes its progress bar to fill the remaining space, with a minimum bar width on narrow terminals. Also drops `DataSize::to_speed`, which becomes dead code once the new layout removes the transfer-speed line.

3. **`refactor: give progress spinners instance-specific messages`**
   Spinners now report which instance or connection they're tracking (e.g. "Cloning foo to bar", "Connecting to baz") instead of a generic message.
